claims.text: A machine-learning framework incorporating defect configurations and oxygen effects will predict the electronic conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed framework is applicable to both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The relevant material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr in an as-cast or annealed condition.
The high-temperature specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, whereas the low-temperature specimen has minimal oxygen contamination.
The ML model will be trained on binary-alloy data augmented with conductivity measurements obtained under realistic defect-bearing and oxygen-contaminated conditions.
Phonon and defect activation are minimal in the 0–200 K regime.
Oxygen-induced defect scattering and thermal activation play substantial roles between 300 and 1200 K.
Relevant microstructural mediators include vacancies, interstitial oxygen atoms, and chemically inhomogeneous regions that disrupt the perfect lattice.
Oxygen atoms can interact with vacancies and otherwise modify defect behavior.
Training on defect- and oxygen-sensitive experimental data enables the ML model to learn additional electron-scattering mechanisms.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical models ignore impurity and defect scattering.
Representing realistic microstructural mediators allows the model to adjust its conductivity predictions accordingly.
The ML model will reduce prediction error by more than 20% relative to analytical models in both temperature regimes.
Oxygen-induced defect scattering will lower high-temperature conductivity relative to an ideal-lattice prediction.
Residual-defect scattering at low temperature will be captured more accurately by the ML model.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical methods systematically overestimate the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The model's applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr in the stated temperature intervals and is unreliable for oxygen concentrations significantly different from approximately 1 wt.%.
Other scattering mechanisms may dominate outside the stated temperature ranges.
The magnitude of the expected accuracy improvement is uncertain because available data are sparse and heterogeneous and because oxygen distributions and defect types may vary.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant error reduction relative to analytical models across both regimes would falsify the proposed accuracy advantage.

contradictions.description: The predicted improvement is defined as a greater-than-20% reduction in error relative to analytical models, but the falsification rule instead invokes prediction deviations greater than 20%. Relative error reduction and absolute deviation are different metrics, so the stated falsification threshold is not the logical complement of the prediction.
